original_question: A normalized basic sequence (x_n) is called a Rosenthal basis when every normalized block sequence of (x_n) has a subsequence equivalent to (x_n). Must every Rosenthal basis be equivalent to the standard unit vector basis of c_0 or of l_p for some 1 <= p < infinity?
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's official problem almost verbatim: it uses the correct notion of a Rosenthal basis, the correct hypothesis on normalized block sequences, and the exact classification target from the paper—equivalence to the standard unit vector basis of c_0 or of ℓ_p for some 1 ≤ p < ∞.
missing_details: State explicitly that (x_n) is a normalized basic sequence in a Banach space X.

For full stand-alone clarity, define a normalized block sequence of (x_n) as a sequence of norm-one finite linear combinations of successive x_i's with strictly increasing, pairwise disjoint supports.
Clarify that 'equivalent' means equivalent as basic sequences.
If one wants complete ambient conventions, specify that X is over the real or complex field, since the paper relies on standard Banach-space terminology without restating the scalar field here.
refined_question: Let X be a real or complex Banach space, and let (x_n) be a normalized basic sequence in X. Say that (x_n) is a Rosenthal basis if every normalized block sequence (v_n) of (x_n) (that is, each v_n is a norm-one finite linear combination of successive x_i's, with successive pairwise disjoint supports) has a subsequence equivalent, as a basic sequence, to (x_n). Is it true that every Rosenthal basis is equivalent to the standard unit vector basis of c_0 or of ℓ_p for some 1 ≤ p < ∞?
justification: The paper introduces this question in Section 4 under the heading "Rosenthal basis problem." Immediately before Problem 3, it recalls the stronger notion of a perfectly homogeneous basic sequence and Zippin's classification theorem (Theorem 5), then says that a Rosenthal basis is the slightly weaker notion obtained by requiring only a subsequence of each normalized block sequence to be equivalent to the original basis. Problem 3 then asks exactly whether every Rosenthal basis must be equivalent to the standard unit vector basis of c_0 or ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p < ∞. The sentence right after Problem 3 records the nearby partial result: the answer is known to be affirmative if there is a uniform constant C such that every normalized block sequence has a C-equivalent subsequence. So your draft is already very close; the main improvements are only to make the ambient Banach-space setting and the block-sequence/equivalence conventions fully explicit.
